Working paper · extended dataset · September 2026

Energy Performance Certificates and Residential Prices Across Five Portuguese Cities

Mengwen Qu · Nuno D. Cortiços

CIAUD, Research Centre for Architecture, Urbanism and Design, Lisbon School of Architecture, Universidade de Lisboa

13,819 raw listings 6,164 cleaned 5 cities Remax · Century 21 · ERA two collections: Aug–Sep · Sep 30

About this study

Does the Portuguese housing market pay for energy performance — and does it pay the same way in every city?

An earlier study by the same authors examined how Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) ratings are capitalized into residential asking prices in three contiguous Lisbon parishes — Lumiar, Benfica and Carnide — and found that each one-class decline in EPC rating was associated with roughly €590/m² less in listed price (R² = 0.44, n = 450). This site extends that analysis to five Portuguese municipalities using 13,819 listings scraped from Remax, Century 21 and ERA Portugal between 3 August and 10 September 2026. After harmonizing the three platforms into one schema and applying the original study's cleaning and coding rules, 6,164 listings remain (5,916 after a 4% two-sided trim on price/m² for the regression).

What the extension adds

The original estimate came from a single, relatively homogeneous stretch of northern Lisbon. The obvious question is whether it generalizes. Adding Sintra, Vila Nova de Gaia, Porto and Cascais trades some of that estimate's precision for external validity, and treats city as an explicit stratifying dimension rather than assuming the market is uniform. Every chart in the original paper is reproduced here twice: pooled across all five cities, and separately for each city.

Key findings

1

The direction is universal; the strength is not. Every city returns a negative, statistically significant EPC coefficient — but it ranges from −€160/m² per class in Sintra to −€565/m² in Lisboa, and R² ranges from 0.02 to 0.17.

2

Pooling costs explanatory power. The five-city pooled fit is ŷ = 7,753 − 414·x with R² = 0.08 — directionally consistent with the original −593 / R² = 0.44, but far noisier once markets with different price levels and stock ages are combined.

3

The premium still exceeds the energy saving. Scaled to a 100 m² unit, the pooled per-class price gap (≈€41,400) runs about four to five times the ten-year cumulative energy-cost gap between adjacent classes — so the EPC premium is not simply capitalized running-cost savings.

4

The regulatory shift holds everywhere. In all five cities the post-2014 REH/NZEB cohort is dominated by classes A and A+, while pre-1990 stock sits in C–E — regulation raised the floor for new build without moving the existing stock.

Listings were excluded if the property was not a residential dwelling unit (land, whole buildings, garages and commercial listings were dropped); if the EPC field was missing, invalid, or marked exempt / in process; if usable area or price was missing; if usable area fell outside 20–500 m²; or if price per square metre fell below €2,000. Price per square metre was recomputed uniformly as price divided by usable area for all three platforms rather than trusting each platform's own displayed figure.

EPC class is coded as an ordered integer following the SCE hierarchy — A+ = 1, A = 2, B = 3, B− = 3.5, C = 4, D = 5, E = 6, F = 7 — and construction year is grouped into the four Portuguese thermal-regulation cohorts: Pre-1990, 1991–2005 (RCCTE 1990), 2006–2013 (RCCTE 2006) and 2014–present (REH/NZEB).

Caveats worth carrying into any reading of these charts

  • Listing prices, not transactions. Asking prices differ from sale prices, and the gap may itself correlate with EPC class.
  • No hedonic controls. Floor level, condition, micro-location and transport access are not controlled for, so omitted-variable bias is present throughout.
  • ERA supplies no construction year. Its listings enter the price–EPC analysis but not the cohort charts, which therefore rest on a smaller subsample.
  • Vila Nova de Gaia lacks Remax coverage in the first collection, and has only 69 dated listings. The 30 September collection fixes this.
  • Off-plan listings are capped. Construction years after 2026 (pre-sale units) are treated as missing, following the robustness check the original manuscript recommends.
  • The energy-cost benchmark is reconstructed from the cost figures stated in the original manuscript, not from an official SCE consumption table.

The spread is the finding. An eight-fold range in R² (0.02 in Sintra to 0.17 in Vila Nova de Gaia) and a 3.5× range in the coefficient means there is no single national figure for what an EPC class is worth — a result the original single-neighbourhood study could not have surfaced.

Cumulative energy cost by EPC class

This calculation depends only on EPC class, not on location, so it is not re-estimated per city. The per-class reference consumption was reconstructed from the cost anchors stated in the original manuscript (roughly €5,500 at A+ and €60,000 at F over ten years, on a 100 m² dwelling at the 2023 tariff of €0.22/kWh) and should be read as indicative rather than as an official SCE benchmark.

Scaled to a 100 m² unit, the pooled coefficient implies roughly €41,400 of listed price per EPC class, against a ten-year energy-cost step of roughly €8,000–11,000 per class from C onward — a price gap around four to five times the cost gap. The original three-parish study put that ratio at about six times.

Platform mix: Remax 1,727 · C21 445 · ERA 394  |  listings with a usable construction year: 1,955 of 2,566

Lisboa contributes 2,566 cleaned listings — 41.6% of the whole five-city sample — at a median of €7,062/m² (IQR €5,665–8,571). It shows the steepest EPC coefficient of the five cities: each one-class decline is associated with roughly €565/m² less in listed price (R² = 0.14).

The shape of that relationship matters as much as its slope. Class medians are not a smooth staircase: A+ (€9,745) sits above A (€7,895), and B (€9,371) and B− (€8,895) sit above both, while C, D, E and F bunch tightly between €6,200 and €6,317. Most of the fitted slope is therefore the gap between the top classes and everything below, not a gradient running through the middle of the market — the same non-monotonic top-class pattern reported in the original three-parish study, where small top-class samples concentrate in prime new developments.

Of the 1,955 Lisboa listings carrying a usable construction year, 1,028 are pre-1990 and 592 are post-2014 — a barbell distribution with a thin middle (193 in 1991–2005, 142 in 2006–2013), consistent with a city that built heavily before the first thermal regulation and again under REH/NZEB, with comparatively little in between.

Platform mix: Remax 755 · ERA 163 · C21 160  |  listings with a usable construction year: 888 of 1,078

Sintra is the clearest counter-example to the pooled result. Across 1,078 cleaned listings at a median of €3,855/m², the EPC coefficient falls to €160/m² per class with an R² of just 0.02. The relationship is still statistically significant (p ≈ 8×10-7, on a sample this size), but it explains roughly two percent of the variation in price — EPC class is close to irrelevant as a price signal here.

The class medians show why: €5,138 (A+), €4,334 (A), €3,936 (B), €3,853 (C), €3,730 (D), €3,968 (F). Below the handful of top-rated units the market is essentially flat, and F-rated stock actually out-prices D. Sintra also has the lowest-rated stock profile of the five cities — only 9.8% of listings are A or A+, while 83.9% fall in C–F, and 735 of its 888 dated listings predate 2006.

The practical implication is that policy calibrated on inner-Lisbon evidence — green mortgage pricing, retrofit payback assumptions — would substantially overstate what an EPC upgrade is worth to a seller in this market.

Vila Nova de Gaia has both the lowest median price (€3,449/m²) and the smallest sample (383 listings, 6.2% of the total) of the five cities. It also returns the highest per-city R² (0.165) on a coefficient of €338/m² per class, with class medians falling cleanly from A (€4,958) through B− (€3,325) to D (€2,960).

That fit should be read with care. The first collection contains no Remax export for Vila Nova de Gaia, so the sample rests entirely on ERA (303 listings) and Century 21 (80) — it is the only city whose data is not triangulated across all three platforms.

Data coverage. Thin cohort base. Only 69 of this city's 383 listings carry a construction year (ERA exports contain no year field, and there is no Remax file for Vila Nova de Gaia), so the cohort charts below rest on a Century 21-only subsample with single-digit cell counts. Read them as indicative at best, not as a profile of the city's stock.

Platform mix: Remax 726 · ERA 409 · C21 136  |  listings with a usable construction year: 684 of 1,271

Porto returns the most orderly EPC–price relationship of the five cities. Across 1,271 listings at a median of €5,092/m², the coefficient is €393/m² per class (R² = 0.144), and the class medians descend almost step for step: €6,053 (A), €5,247 (B), €5,469 (B−), €4,333 (C), €4,240 (D), €3,882 (E), €3,526 (F). Only the A+/A pair is inverted, and only slightly.

Porto also has the highest share of top-rated stock in the study: 40.6% of its listings are A or A+, against 20.0% in Lisboa and 9.8% in Sintra. Of the 684 listings with a usable construction year, 415 are post-2014, so the sample skews strongly toward recent construction — which is very likely what produces both the high A-class share and the clean gradient, since cohort and EPC class are tightly correlated in Portuguese stock.

Platform mix: Remax 647 · C21 129 · ERA 90  |  listings with a usable construction year: 753 of 866

Cascais is the most expensive market in the study (median €7,129/m², IQR €5,437–9,120) and the one where location most visibly overrides energy performance. The fitted coefficient is €410/m² per class, but R² is only 0.083.

The bottom of the ladder is the reason. The F-class median (€7,500) sits above C (€6,462), D (€6,034) and E (€6,303), and the B-class median (€9,932) is the highest of any class in any city in the study. In a coastal prime market, older low-rated stock in the best locations comfortably out-prices newer, better-rated units further inland — the locational-offset effect the original paper described for central Lisbon, but considerably stronger here.

Cascais's cohort profile is the most evenly spread of the five: of 753 dated listings, 231 are pre-1990, 157 from 1991–2005, 93 from 2006–2013 and 272 post-2014.

A rolling collection, not a single-day snapshot. This is the dataset behind every other tab on this site.

This collection was gathered platform by platform over five weeks while the scraper was still being developed, so it is not a snapshot of one moment. The dates recorded in the files themselves are:

Collection dates as recorded in each export.
PlatformCollectedDetail
Remax3–29 AugustLisboa parishes 3 Aug, Sintra 11 Aug, Porto 14 Aug, Cascais 15 and 29 Aug
Century 2131 Augustall five cities in one run
ERA10 Septemberall five cities in one run
Why it is still treated as a single cross-section. Prices were effectively static across this interval: of the listings that appear in both this collection and the 30 September snapshot, 90% had no price change at all, and the median change was 0.0% in every one of the five cities. Pooling the five weeks into one cross-section is therefore an evidenced choice rather than an assumption — but it is a pooled cross-section, not a snapshot, and nothing here should be read as describing the market on a particular day.

Pooled across all five cities, this wave gives ŷ = 5,795 €/m² median and an EPC coefficient of −414 €/m² per one-class decline (R² = 0.08, n = 5,916).

Known limitations of this collection

  • It spans five weeks, with the platforms collected on different dates (above). Any comparison against a later collection has a different time gap for each platform — 20 days for ERA, up to eight weeks for Remax.
  • Remax had no Vila Nova de Gaia export. VNG rests on Century 21 and ERA alone — 383 cleaned listings, the smallest of the five, and only 18% of them carry a construction year.
  • ERA publishes no construction year, which caps cohort analysis at 71% of the sample. Checked directly against ERA listing pages: the field does not exist at source, so it cannot be scraped.
  • 446 Remax rows (6.1% of that platform's raw export) carry a corrupt collection date of 1970-01-01, concentrated in two files. It affects only the date stamp, not the price, area or EPC fields, so those listings remain usable for the price analysis.
  • No coordinates on any platform, so micro-location could not be controlled for.

Unlike the first collection, every one of the fifteen exports in this one carries the same date — 30 September 2026. It is the first properly contemporaneous cross-section in the study, and the baseline against which later collections can be compared as a genuine time series.

It was processed through a rule set identical to the first collection's, so any difference between them is data rather than method. These numbers are not used by the other tabs: the earlier analysis was deliberately left in place, and this collection serves as an independent check on it — see the comparison tab.

Pooled across all five cities, this wave gives ŷ = 5,566 €/m² median and an EPC coefficient of −350 €/m² per one-class decline (R² = 0.06, n = 6,627).

What improved in this collection

  • Remax now covers Vila Nova de Gaia (639 cleaned listings). VNG's sample nearly tripled and its construction-year coverage went from 18% to 53%, so its numbers are finally worth reading.
  • ERA listings now carry coordinates (83–99% filled). The original study noted that location could not be georeferenced because the platforms withhold street addresses; for ERA that is no longer true.
  • Listings are now tracked between collections — each carries a status (new / existing), a first-seen date and its previous price, with separate files logging additions, delistings, price adjustments and EPC changes.
  • ERA still publishes no construction year, so that limitation is unchanged.

Comparing the two collections

Every city's result holds across two independently gathered datasets. That is a robustness check, not a measurement of change over time — the two collections do not sit a fixed interval apart.

What this comparison can and cannot show. The first collection was gathered over five weeks (Remax 3–29 August, Century 21 31 August, ERA 10 September); the second is a single day, 30 September. The gap between them is therefore 20 days for ERA listings and up to eight weeks for Remax. That is ample for testing whether the findings reproduce on independently collected data, which is what this tab does. It is not a clean basis for measuring how the market moved, because the interval differs by platform. A proper time series starts from the 30 September snapshot and its successors.

Both collections were processed through an identical rule set, so any difference between them is data, not method. Four of the five cities moved by less than 1% in sample size. Vila Nova de Gaia grew from 383 to 1,017 listings for one reason only: Remax had no Vila Nova de Gaia file in the first collection and now covers it. That is new platform coverage, not a change in the market.

Does the headline result replicate?

How to read: negative = buyers pay more for better EPC. β is the OLS slope of price/m² on EPC code (A+=1, A=2, B=3, B−=3.5, C=4, D=5, E=6, F=7) after 4% trim — not a price level, so it cannot be positive. E.g. Lisboa Sep β=−568 means each 1-class worsening is associated with −€568/m² (≈−€56,800 per class for 100 m², ≈8% of median). −565 to −568 is a €3 steeper discount, not a price rise — confidence intervals overlap, i.e. no change.

The pattern holds in the second collection. Vila Nova de Gaia is now worth reading: it had only 63 dated listings in the first against 489 in the second, and with that sample the EPC effect disappears entirely once building age is controlled.

A composition trap

Pooled medians move when the city mix moves. The pooled median price fell from €5,795 to €5,566/m² between the two, which reads like a falling market. It is not. Among the listings present in both the median moved 0.0% in every city — the entire drop is Vila Nova de Gaia, the cheapest of the five, contributing 634 more listings. Comparisons across collections have to be made per city, or on matched listings.

What changed between the collections

Of the 4,925 listings present in both, 4,430 did not change price at all. Of those that moved, 416 were cuts and 79 were rises, with a median move of -4.1%. Only 20 listings changed EPC class. Alongside them, 1,239 listings from the first collection had been delisted and 1,980 new ones had appeared — high churn, flat prices, over an interval of 20 days to eight weeks depending on the platform.

Extends: Qu, M. & Cortiços, N. D. Energy Performance Certificates and Residential Prices in Three Lisbon Neighborhoods: A Cross-Cohort Analysis of Lumiar, Benfica and Carnide (manuscript EM26-0161E, in review). CIAUD, Lisbon School of Architecture, Universidade de Lisboa.

This site presents a five-city extension of that study's methodology and is not itself peer reviewed. Charts generated with pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib and seaborn.
